6.11 Inflation and Real Returns

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

A household’s goals are about buying things in the future: a home, education, life in retirement. Their prices rise with inflation, so planning should use real returns (real interest rate), not nominal ones.

Planning in real terms

Section titled “Planning in real terms”

People tend to think in nominal amounts: a 3% raise feels like getting richer even if prices also rose 3%. This tendency is called money illusion. The way to avoid it in household planning is to state every goal in today’s purchasing power, use real rates of return after inflation, and read the results in today’s purchasing power too. Capital market assumptions (4.11 Capital Market Assumptions) are usually given as real returns.

Planning must also separate incomes and expenses that adjust with inflation from those that do not: Social Security adjusts for inflation; most private pensions and ordinary annuities are fixed nominal amounts; and the payment on a fixed-rate mortgage is a fixed nominal amount too.

Check C1
A 65-year-old retiree has a pension of 3,000 dollars a month that does not adjust for inflation. Following the pattern in Figure 1-1, with 3% inflation, which statement is most accurate?
Will 3,000 dollars buy as much in 20 years as today? Look at the readout for 20 years.
Inflation compounds, and each year removes about 3% of the remaining purchasing power. Roughly what is 11.0320\frac{1}{1.03^{20}}1.03201​?

Which assets protect against inflation

Section titled “Which assets protect against inflation”

Assets protect against inflation in different ways, and one must distinguish expected from unexpected inflation, and the short run from the long run:

  • Cash and Treasury bills: their rates adjust to expected inflation and keep up in the short run, but their real return is often near 0.
  • Nominal bonds: unexpected inflation lowers their real value, more so the longer the maturity (3.4 Interest Rate Risk).
  • Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS): the principal adjusts with the CPI, guaranteeing a real return if held to maturity (3.6 Credit Risk).
  • The I bond (Series I savings bond): a savings bond issued by the US Treasury whose rate combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate reset every six months from the CPI. I bonds do not trade in a market; they can be redeemed at their accrued value, so their nominal value never falls; they must be held at least 1 year, and redeeming within 5 years forfeits the last 3 months of interest; each person can buy at most 10,000 dollars a year; interest is taxed federally only at redemption and is exempt from state tax. I bonds bought from November 2026 to April 2027 have a fixed rate of 1.40% and a composite rate of 5.51%.
  • Stocks: companies’ revenues and assets rise with prices, so stocks keep up with inflation in the long run, but in the short run unexpected inflation often comes with rising rates and falling valuations (2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices).
  • Commodities and real estate: somewhat positively related to inflation (5.5 Alternative Assets), but very volatile themselves.
  • Fixed-rate liabilities: inflation lightens their real burden, a hedge for the borrower (6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance).

What two parts make up the I bond's composite rate? Which part is the real return after inflation? Which number should be compared with the TIPS real yield?

Matching retirement spending with TIPS

Section titled “Matching retirement spending with TIPS”

Most spending in retirement rises with prices; it is a real liability. Matching it with real assets carries the least risk: for example a ladder of TIPS with different maturities, one maturing each year to provide that year’s real spending (Exercises Question 2). This is the same idea as immunization, matching liabilities by duration (3.4 Interest Rate Risk), with a real liability in place of a nominal one. 6.12 Goals-Based Investing extends this idea to all of a household’s goals.

Check C4
A retiree wants a fixed amount of spending money in today's prices each year for the next 10 years. Compared with holding an intermediate nominal bond fund, a ladder of TIPS maturing one per year is better because:
Their expected returns depend on actual versus breakeven inflation (3.6 Credit Risk). Is the ladder's advantage a higher return or lower risk?
A bond fund can be sold at any time. The issue is what it fetches when sold, and whether that covers the year's real spending.

Personal inflation

Section titled “Personal inflation”

The CPI measures the average price change of a basket of goods and services bought by urban consumers (consumer price index), but every household spends differently. Retirees spend more on health care and housing, whose prices often rise faster than average; households with mortgages are affected differently by rising home prices than renters are. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes an experimental index weighted by the spending of households aged 62 and over (CPI-E). Social Security is adjusted by the CPI-W; the 2026 adjustment was 2.8%.

Check C5
If the CPI rose 2.8% over a year, then every retiree's cost of living rose by about 2.8% that year.
The CPI is the average price of which basket? Is a retiree's spending the same as that basket?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Plan in today’s purchasing power and real returns, avoiding money illusion; separate incomes and expenses that adjust with inflation from those that do not.
  • Nominal bonds suffer from unexpected inflation; TIPS and I bonds protect real value; stocks keep up with inflation in the long run but not necessarily in the short run; fixed-rate liabilities favor the borrower.
  • Retirement spending is a real liability that a TIPS ladder can match.
  • Personal inflation can differ from the CPI, especially for retirees.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A 35-year-old investor sees an online calculator saying: "To retire at 65, you need 2 million dollars." The calculator assumes 3% inflation and a 7% nominal return.
(a) What is 2 million dollars in 30 years worth in today's purchasing power (thousand dollars)? What real return corresponds to the 7% nominal return?
(b) He says: "At 4% a year, 2 million dollars gives 80,000 dollars a year, enough for my current 70,000 dollars a year of spending." Evaluate this statement, and say how to avoid this kind of mistake.
Question 2
A 65-year-old retiree wants 40,000 dollars (in today's purchasing power) at the end of each of the next 10 years. TIPS at all maturities yield 1.8% real, and nominal Treasuries at all maturities yield 4.2%.
(a) How much does a TIPS ladder providing this spending cost today (thousand dollars)? How much does a nominal Treasury ladder paying a fixed 40,000 nominal dollars a year cost? With 3% inflation, how much would nominal Treasuries cost to pay the inflation-adjusted amounts 40×1.03t40 \times 1.03^t40×1.03t?
(b) He says: "The nominal ladder costs only 320,000 dollars and TIPS 360,000, so obviously choose nominal." Evaluate this statement.
